title: Cosmic calibration
caption: ALMA antennas under the Moon, ALMA Operations Support Facility, Chile
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Moon shines brightly above the Operations Support Facility (OSF) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) in this photograph, while two 12-meter antenna dishes stand in front. The OSF sits at 2900 meters in the Chilean Andes and is a hub of ALMA activity. It houses staff and contractors and runs all the scientific operations for the array's daily work.

The two antennas were brought down from their observing site for a check-up on special calibration pads. The tests cover computers and motors, and they make sure each dish surface is accurate to within less than a human hair's thickness. They also confirm that a dish can point precisely enough to spot a golf ball 15 kilometers away.
Afterwards the antennas will return to the Chajnantor Plateau, at 5000 meters. Each weighs around 100 tonnes, and two huge custom-built transporters named Otto and Lore will carry them back.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of ALMA's Operations Support Facility at night with the Moon overhead. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can make the Moon and its surroundings look brighter or more evenly lit than they would to the eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: Otto and Lore have a top speed of 12 kilometers per hour. Once back in position on the plateau, the antennas will rejoin the rest of the array and resume their observations. The photograph is credited to A. Duro and ESO.
alt: Two large dish antennas in the foreground with buildings behind them and a bright Moon in the sky above.
